Options: B) A group of similar cells performing a common function
Explanation: Tissue: group of similar cells working together to perform a specific function. E.g., muscle tissue (contraction), nerve tissue (conduction).

QuestionText: Plant tissues are broadly classified as:
Explanation: Plant tissues: meristematic (dividing cells, growth) and permanent (non-dividing, specialized functions).

Options: A) Dead cells with thick walls
Explanation: Meristematic (embryonic) tissue: actively dividing undifferentiated cells. Found at growing tips (shoot apex, root apex) and lateral cambium. Responsible for plant growth.

Options: B) Water and mineral salts from roots to leaves
Explanation: Xylem: complex vascular tissue transporting water and dissolved minerals upward (roots → stem → leaves). Made of vessel elements, tracheids, fibres, parenchyma.

Options: B) Food (photosynthates) from leaves to other parts
Explanation: Phloem: complex tissue transporting food (sucrose, amino acids) made in leaves to other parts — bidirectional (up and down). Sieve tubes + companion cells.

Options: B) Living simple tissue with thin-walled cells for storage
Explanation: Parenchyma: most common plant tissue. Living cells, thin cell walls, large vacuoles. Functions: storage (starch, water), photosynthesis (chlorenchyma), healing.

Options: B) Protective outer layer of cells
Explanation: Epidermis: outermost protective layer of cells in plants. Secretes cuticle (waxy layer). Stomata in leaf epidermis control gas exchange and water loss.

Options: B) Dead cells with suberin that protect the stem
Explanation: Cork: dead cells impregnated with suberin (waxy waterproof substance). Forms bark of older stems. Protects from water loss, mechanical damage, pathogens.
Epithelial tissue: forms covering/lining of body surfaces, organs, cavities. Functions: protection, secretion, absorption, excretion. Tightly packed cells.
Connective tissue: diverse tissues with cells embedded in extracellular matrix. Types: blood, bone, cartilage, adipose (fat), fibrous connective, areolar.

Options: C) Voluntary and under conscious control
Explanation: Skeletal (striated) muscle: voluntary (conscious control), attached to bones, multinucleate, striped appearance. Smooth muscle: involuntary (internal organs). Cardiac: involuntary (heart).
Smooth muscle: involuntary, no striations, uninucleate, spindle-shaped. Found in walls of internal organs: digestive tract, blood vessels, uterus, bladder.
Cardiac muscle: involuntary (heartbeat auto-regulated), striated, branched, with intercalated discs (special junctions). Only in heart walls.
Neurons: conducting electrical signals. Parts: dendrites (receive signals), cell body, axon (transmit signals), synaptic knobs (pass signal to next neuron).
Blood is a fluid connective tissue. Cells (RBCs, WBCs, platelets) suspended in plasma (matrix). Functions: transport, immune defence, clotting.

Options: B) Calcium and phosphate salts in matrix
Explanation: Bone: hardened connective tissue. Matrix of collagen fibres + calcium phosphate [Ca₃(PO₄)₂] and calcium carbonate → gives hardness. Bone cells = osteocytes.

Options: B) Ear, nose tip, ends of bones (joints)
Explanation: Cartilage: flexible but firm connective tissue. Found at joint surfaces, ear pinna, nose tip, trachea rings, intervertebral discs. Cells = chondrocytes; matrix = chondrin.
Adipose (fat) tissue: stores triglycerides (fat). Insulates body from cold, cushions organs, stores energy. Fat cells = adipocytes.

QuestionText: Sclerenchyma is a plant tissue with:
Options: B) Dead cells, very thick lignified walls — provides support
Explanation: Sclerenchyma: dead cells with thick, lignified walls. Provides rigid support. Two types: sclereid (stone cells) and fibres (long, like in jute, hemp, flax).

QuestionText: Collenchyma differs from sclerenchyma in that it:
Options: B) Is living with unevenly thickened walls — flexible support
C) Is the same as parenchyma
Explanation: Collenchyma: living cells with unevenly thickened (cellulose) walls. Provides flexible mechanical support. Found in leaf stalks, stems. Can photosynthesise if has chloroplasts.
Guard cells: paired cells in leaf epidermis surrounding stomata (pores). Change shape to open/close stomata — controlling gas exchange and transpiration.
Skeletal muscle fibres: long (up to 30 cm), cylindrical, multinucleate (formed from fusion of many cells = syncytium). Each fibre = one muscle cell.

QuestionText: The epidermis of animals (skin) is primarily:
Explanation: Skin epidermis: stratified squamous epithelium. Multiple layers; outermost cells are dead, flat, keratinised. Provides waterproof barrier against pathogens.

Options: B) Loose connective tissue filling spaces between organs
Explanation: Areolar tissue: loosely arranged fibres (collagen and elastin) + various cells. Fills spaces between organs, supports epithelium, contains blood vessels and nerves.

QuestionText: The axon of a neuron is covered by:
Explanation: Myelin sheath: lipid-rich covering around axon by Schwann cells. Insulates axon, speeds up impulse conduction (saltatory conduction). Absent in unmyelinated neurons.
Tendon: dense connective tissue (collagen fibres) connecting muscle to bone. Ligament: connects bone to bone. Both are inelastic (collagen dominant).

Options: B) Daytime (when guard cells are turgid)
Explanation: Stomata open during day: light → guard cells absorb water → become turgid → open. Close at night to prevent water loss. Also close during drought.

QuestionText: Phloem transports food in which direction?
Explanation: Phloem transport is bidirectional — from source (leaves) to sinks (roots, fruits, growing tips). Can go both up and down simultaneously in different sieve tubes.

QuestionText: Fibrous connective tissue (tendons, ligaments) has mainly:
Explanation: Dense (fibrous) connective tissue: mainly collagen fibres → great tensile strength, little stretch. Tendons and ligaments resist pulling forces. Elastin fibres in elastic ligaments.

QuestionText: The function of the cuticle in plants is:
Options: B) Preventing excess water loss (waterproof waxy layer)
Explanation: Cuticle: waxy layer secreted by epidermis over aerial plant surfaces. Prevents excessive water loss by transpiration. Thick cuticle in desert plants (xerophytes).

Options: B) Differentiated cells that have stopped dividing (specialised)
Explanation: Permanent tissues: derived from meristematic tissues that have differentiated for specific functions. May be simple (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma) or complex (xylem, phloem).

Options: A) The speed of water flow
B) Surface area for water absorption
Explanation: Root hairs: extensions of root epidermal cells. Greatly increase surface area for water and mineral absorption from soil. Not separate cells — extensions of epidermal cells.

Options: B) Have perforated end walls (sieve plates) for transport
Explanation: Sieve tube elements: living cells with perforated end walls (sieve plates). Lack nucleus at maturity. Companion cells assist their function. Food flows through sieve plates.
Ligaments: more elastin fibres → more elastic/stretchy → allows joint movement. Tendons: mostly collagen → inelastic → transmit muscle force efficiently.
Red bone marrow: site of haematopoiesis — formation of all blood cells (RBCs, WBCs, platelets) from stem cells. Yellow marrow stores fat.

QuestionText: Meristem at the tip of root and shoot is called:
Explanation: Apical meristem: at tips of root and shoot → primary growth (increase in length). Lateral meristem (cambium): secondary growth (girth). Intercalary: at nodes (grass regrowth).

QuestionText: The longest cells in the human body are:
Explanation: Neurons: can be extremely long. Sciatic nerve (hip to foot): axon up to 1 metre long! Muscle fibres can be 30 cm. Most cells are microscopic.

QuestionText: Vascular cambium in plants is responsible for:
Explanation: Lateral meristem (vascular cambium): produces secondary xylem (wood) and secondary phloem → increases stem diameter (girth). This is why trees have annual rings.

QuestionText: Muscle is to contraction as nerve is to:
Explanation: Muscle = specialised for contraction. Nerve tissue = specialised for conduction of electrical impulses. Each tissue type is specialised for one primary function.
Ciliated epithelium: cells with hair-like cilia on surface. In trachea — cilia sweep mucus (with trapped dust/bacteria) upward to throat. Also in oviduct (moves egg).

QuestionText: Simple squamous epithelium (single flat layer) is found in:
Options: B) Alveoli (air sacs of lungs) and blood vessel lining
Explanation: Simple squamous: single layer of flat cells. Good for diffusion and filtration. Found in alveoli (gas exchange), blood vessel lining (endothelium), glomerulus of kidney.

Options: B) Fluid in lymph vessels (derived from interstitial fluid)
Explanation: Lymph: colourless fluid in lymphatic vessels. Derived from interstitial fluid (leaked from blood capillaries). Transports digested fat from intestine, returns excess fluid to blood, contains lymphocytes (immune).

QuestionText: The cell wall of plant cells is made of:
Explanation: Plant cell wall: primarily cellulose (a polysaccharide). Fungi: chitin. Bacteria: peptidoglycan. Provides rigid support.

QuestionText: Bark (outer covering of trees) is formed by:
Explanation: Cork cambium (phellogen): lateral meristem producing cork (outer bark). Secondary growth adds girth; cork replaces epidermis in older stems.

QuestionText: Glands secrete substances. They are a type of:
Explanation: Glands: specialised epithelial cells. Exocrine glands (ducts, e.g., sweat, salivary). Endocrine glands (ductless, hormones, e.g., thyroid, adrenal).

QuestionText: Striations in muscle cells are due to:
Options: B) Regular arrangement of contractile proteins (actin and myosin)
Explanation: Striations: alternating dark (A) and light (I) bands from regular arrangement of thick myosin and thin actin filaments in sarcomeres.

QuestionText: The vascular bundles in plants contain:
Explanation: Vascular bundles: contain xylem (water transport) and phloem (food transport) together. In dicots: phloem outside, xylem inside. Forms the vascular system.

QuestionText: Heart muscle differs from skeletal muscle in being:
Options: B) Striated and involuntary with intercalated discs
Explanation: Cardiac: striated (like skeletal) but involuntary (like smooth). Has intercalated discs (allow rapid spread of electrical signals). Never fatigues.

QuestionText: Which type of epithelium is found in the kidney tubules?
Explanation: Cuboidal epithelium: cube-shaped cells. Found in kidney tubules, thyroid gland, salivary glands. Functions in secretion and absorption.

QuestionText: Annual rings in wood are formed by:
Options: B) Activity of lateral (vascular) meristem varying seasonally
Explanation: Annual rings: alternating bands of large-celled spring wood and small-celled autumn wood. Reflect seasonal activity of vascular cambium. Count rings = age of tree.
